question: What procedure is eﬀective at simultaneously treating dissociated vertical deviation and inferior oblique overaction?
explanation: Dissociated vertical deviation (DVD) is an innervational disorder in which either eye slowly drifts upward and outward with extortion when the eye is occluded or there is visual inattention. It typically develops by age 2 years and is commonly associated with infantile strabismus, typically esotropia or exotropia (50%). Treatment of DVD is indicated when the deviation is noticeable (more than 6–8 prism diopters) or is present frequently during the day. Treatments include optical penalization for unilateral or highly asymmetric bilateral DVD or vertical muscle surgery. Large superior rectus muscle recessions can be eﬀective at treating DVD, titrated based on the amount of the hypertropia and the symmetry of the DVD. Inferior rectus muscle resection or plication can help treat residual DVD. In cases of DVD and inferior oblique overaction, inferior oblique muscle anterior transposition has been shown to be eﬀective. Inferior oblique myectomy is eﬀective at treating inferior oblique overaction without DVD.

explanation: Pseudoesotropia occurs when there is an optical illusion of crossing of the eyes, but the ocular alignment is in fact orthophoric. It is seen in the setting of a ﬂat, broad, nasal bridge, epicanthal folds, a narrow interpupillary distance, or negative angle kappa. question: What is the leading cause of vision loss in the world, as well as a leading cause of visual impairment?
explanation: Cataract Cataract is the leading cause of vision loss in the world. The World Health Organization (WHO) has estimated that more than 20 million people are blind due to cataract and that the condition causes 51% of blindness worldwide. The majority of cases (up to 90%) of blindness due to cataract are found in developing areas. Cataract is also the leading cause of visual impairment, with 33% of the world’s population experiencing decreased vision because of this disorder; only refractive error refractive error has a greater impact in this regard. As the leading cause of irreversible blindness in the world, glaucoma glaucoma also poses signiﬁcant public health problem. It has been estimated that by 2020, approximately 80 million people worldwide will have glaucoma, with 11.2 million bilaterally blind as a result. A meta-analysis estimated that the global prevalence is about 3.5%.

question: While isolating rectus muscles during routine strabismus surgery, the anesthesiologist reports that the patient is experiencing severe bradycardia. What is the preferred initial management?

options.A: Continue working while the anesthesiologist administers intravenous atropine.
options.B: Finish isolating muscles as quickly as possible and recheck vital signs.
options.C: Administer additional retrobulbar anesthesia while the assistant infraducts the eye.
options.D: Release any tension on the muscle and monitor for improved heart rate.

explanation: This scenario describes the oculocardiac reﬂex, which is a decline in heart rate due to traction on the conjunctiva, globe, or extraocular muscles, particularly the medial rectus. Asystole is the most severe form of the oculocardiac reﬂex. If muscles will be manipulated during a case, the surgeon must keep this in mind, and the anesthesiologist should be notiﬁed. If a patient has signiﬁcant bradycardia, the surgeon should be prepared to release any traction on the muscle(s) immediately. Retrobulbar anesthesia, once achieved, can prevent the aﬀerent end of the reﬂex, but the oculocardiac reﬂex may occur during administration of the block. Intravenous atropine can be administered to protect against bradycardia, but release of tension on the muscle is the ﬁrst step. simultaneous prism and cover test A. 33% Your Answer red glass test B. 1% Explanation & Notes Discussion BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What clinical test is most useful for measuring heterotropia separate from any underlying heterophoria?
explanation: Tests of ocular alignment can measure either the heterotropia or the combined heterotropia and heterophoria. The simultaneous prism- cover test measures the actual heterotropia separate from the heterophoria during binocular viewing and is especially useful in cases of monoﬁxation syndrome. The Lancaster red-green test, alternate prism-cover test, and double Maddox rod test all disrupt fusion and measure the combined heterotropia and heterophoria.

question: What best explains the diﬀerence in the measurements dependent on which eye is ﬁxing?

options.A: A primary deviation is greater than a secondary deviation.
options.B: There is a fracture of the nasal wall of the left orbit.
options.C: The patient has developed myasthenia gravis.
options.D: A secondary deviation is greater than a primary deviation.

explanation: The ﬁndings are consistent with a weakness of the left lateral rectus. The amount of innervation to synergist muscles is determined by the ﬁxating eye. The primary deviation is the amount of strabismus present with the normal eye ﬁxating. The secondary deviation is the amount of strabismus with the paretic eye ﬁxating. Since the deviation was greater with the left eye ﬁxating, it was the result of secondary deviation. Increased innervation to the weak left lateral rectus is necessary to allow the paretic eye to move to the point of ﬁxation, which creates the same extra innervation to the yoke right medial rectus. This increases the amount of esotropia measured. A secondary deviation is always greater than primary deviation. Myasthenia gravis is not likely, as there was no ﬂuctuation during the day, and ptosis was not present. A nasal orbital wall fracture could cause decreased abduction, but it was ruled out by the normal CT scan.

question: What is the most common ophthalmologic manifestation of abusive head trauma?
explanation: Retinal hemorrhages are the cardinal manifestation of abusive head trauma (AHT, formerly termed shaken baby syndrome). The incidence of retinal hemorrhages in AHT is approximately 80%. Classically, children with AHT have retinal hemorrhages that are multilayered: preretinal, intraretinal, and subretinal. Papilledema occurs in less than 10% of cases of AHT. Cranial nerve paresis and exudative retinal detachment are not commonly associated with AHT.

question: From what material are optic nerve drusen believed to develop?
explanation: Drusen of the optic nerve head are calciﬁc, usually bilateral, deposits embedded within the parenchyma of crowded discs and abnormal vasculature. Evidence suggests that abnormal axonal metabolism leads to mitochondrial calciﬁcation and drusen formation. Hard macular drusen are composed of hyaline material.

question: A child with cognitive impairment, seizures, and hypomelanotic macules presents for routine eye care. What intraocular ﬁnding is most likely to be observed?
explanation: The classic triad of tuberous sclerosis (known as Vogt triad) includes cognitive impairment, seizures, and facial angioﬁbromas. Facial angioﬁbromas are not usually present in young children, but hypomelanotic macules called "ash-leaf spots" are. The most frequent BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: Leukemia has the highest likelihood to inﬁltrate what ocular tissue(s)?
explanation: Leukemia is most likely to inﬁltrate the retina and choroid. Retinal hemorrhages in the nerve ﬁber layer are the most likely ﬁnding. Optic nerve inﬁltration may occur and requires emergent treatment, due to BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 30-year-old man presents for evaluation of one eye turning out when he is tired. He has experienced this for several years. Initial evaluation demonstrates orthophoria. Upon cover testing, an exodeviation becomes present, although he is able to resume fusion with blinking. How is his exodeviation most accurately described?
explanation: This is a case of intermittent exotropia. The grading of control of an intermittent exotropia is usually classiﬁed as poor, fair, or good. The patient is initially orthophoric, and by history also has periods of orthophoric alignment. The exotropia becomes manifest after disruption of fusion with cover testing, and fusion can be resumed with blinking, which indicates fair control. Poor control of an intermittent exotropia is indicated by periods of prolonged manifest exotropia occurring spontaneously, while good control is indicated by an exodeviation that is manifested only by cover testing and in which fusion can rapidly be regained without blinking or reﬁxating. An exophoria would be suggested by an exodeviation that is present only with complete disruption of binocular vision (eg, alternate cover test).

question: A patient presents with orthophoria at distance and 30 prism diopters (30Δ) of esotropia at near. The cycloplegic refraction is -0.25 sphere OU. What is the most common treatment used to decrease the near deviation?

options.B: bifocals with -0.25 for distance and +3.00 add

explanation: In cases of high accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) ratio, excessive convergence tone results from accommodation, leading to esotropia at near. The most common treatment for high AC/A ratio includes bifocals with a +3.00 add to decrease the accommodative drive. Cholinesterase inhibitors, such as echothiophate iodide, and surgery are other treatment modalities. Over-minused myopic glasses and cycloplegics increase accommodative drive and worsen the esotropia.

question: What is the most likely beneﬁt of strabismus surgery for congenital nystagmus with a null point?
explanation: Indications for strabismus surgery include improving functional vision by decreasing diplopia, relieving asthenopia, improving ocular alignment and establishing or restoring stereopsis, expanding binocular visual ﬁelds, or shifting best vision to a more central location (and by extension, reducing head turn). In congenital nystagmus with a null point, the null point may not be in primary gaze, and patients will adopt a compensatory head turn. A Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure shifts the null point to primary position. While some forms of congenital nystagmus are associated with strabismus, many may present in isolation. Strabismus surgery for nystagmus is not considered cosmetic, and strabismus surgery for nystagmus would not restore stereopsis.

question: A patient is diagnosed with inferior oblique muscle overaction. What would the most likely ﬁndings be on versions testing?

options.A: overelevation of the aﬀected eye in adduction
options.B: overelevation of the aﬀected eye in adduction and abduction
options.C: overelevation of the aﬀected eye in abduction
options.D: overelevation of the aﬀected eye in primary position

explanation: The actions of the inferior oblique vary in diﬀerent gazes because the muscle axis is not parallel with the visual axis. Therefore, in primary position the primary action is extorsion. In adduction, the primary action is as an elevator. In abduction, the primary action is extorsion. Therefore, an overacting inferior oblique will show overelevation in adduction primarily.

question: A 3-year-old girl has had recurrent episodes of redness and discharge in both eyes. The external examination of her right eye is abnormal, as shown. What type of protein deﬁciency can lead to this condition?
explanation: The ﬁgure demonstrates ﬁrm, yellow, woody-like pseudomembranous lesions on the tarsal conjunctivae. This appearance is of ligneous conjunctivitis, a rare disorder associated with a systemic plasminogen deﬁciency. Fibrinogen (factor I) is needed for platelet aggregation, and therefore patients with ﬁbrinogen deﬁciency present with a bleeding disorder. Hexosaminidase A deﬁciency is found in patients with Tay- Sachs disease; α-galactosidase A deﬁciency is found in patients with Fabry disease.

question: What is the preferred laboratory testing for a child with a unilateral congenital cataract?

options.D: TORCH titers (toxoplasmosis, other agents, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex)

explanation: Unilateral cataracts are not usually associated with occult systemic or metabolic disease; laboratory tests are therefore not warranted. It is important to note that bilateral cataracts can have signiﬁcant asymmetry, however, so deferring laboratory tests should be done with caution. In cases of bilateral cataracts, multiple components of the history and physical examination, rather than a battery of tests (a "shotgun" approach), can be useful for directed laboratory investigations. Part of the evaluation of pediatric cataracts should focus on cataract morphology (eg, nuclear, lamellar, anterior polar, posterior lenticonus, etc.). Family history is useful in some cases (isolated inherited cataracts are usually autosomal dominant). Other features that could suggest a need for directed testing include external appearance (eg, many craniofacial syndromes are associated with cataracts, as are chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome, trisomy 13, and trisomy 18), history of renal disease (eg, Alport syndrome or Lowe syndrome), or history of metabolic disorders (eg, diabetes mellitus, Fabry disease, Wilson disease, etc). TORCH titers can also be useful in certain circumstances.

question: What is the most appropriate surgery to perform for a V-pattern esotropia with no inferior oblique overaction?

options.A: bilateral lateral rectus resection with inferior transposition (inferoplacement)
options.B: bilateral medial rectus recession with inferior transposition (inferoplacement)
options.C: unilateral medial rectus recession and lateral rectus resection with inferior transposition (inferoplacement)
options.D: bilateral medial rectus recession with superior transposition (superoplacement)

explanation: In a V-pattern esotropia, the medial rectus muscles can be recessed and moved toward the apex of the deviation, which would be inferiorly in this case. Lateral muscles should be moved away from the apex of the deviation. A useful mnemonic is MALE: medial rectus muscle to the apex, lateral rectus muscle to the empty space. When horizontal muscle recession-resection is performed, displacement should be in opposite directions, but this will cause symptomatic torsion if the patient has vision in the eye.

question: A 2-month-old child has an abnormality of the cornea as shown. What additional corneal ﬁnding would conﬁrm the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A large corneal diameter, along with horizontal or curvilinear breaks in Descemet membrane, indicates primary congenital glaucoma. Vertical or oblique breaks in Descemet membrane are seen in birth trauma from forceps delivery. Iridocorneal adhesions are suggestive of Peters anomaly. Absent Descemet membrane results in corneal edema with a normal corneal diameter. Central cornea thickness (CCT) is typically higher in infants with glaucoma.

question: What nerve typically provides aberrant innervation to the levator in Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome?
explanation: Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome is the result of a congenital trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis of the jaw and levator muscles. The motor division of the trigeminal nerve aberrantly provides innervation in this scenario. The ptotic eyelid elevates with opening of the mouth or movement of the jaw to the contralateral side. Descemet membrane folds.

question: What is the earliest sign of anterior segment ischemia following strabismus surgery?
explanation: The blood supply to the anterior segment of the eye is partially supplied by the anterior ciliary arteries that travel within the 4 rectus muscles. Simultaneous rectus muscle surgery, especially on 3 or 4 muscles (but also 2 muscles in patients with poor circulation) can result in anterior segment ischemia. The earliest sign of this complication is cells and ﬂare in the anterior chamber, with more severe cases causing corneal epithelial edema, Descemet membrane folds, and an irregular pupil. In the most extreme cases, anterior segment necrosis and phthisis bulbi can occur.

question: A 6-year-old girl presents for her annual eye examination and glasses update. Retinoscopy demonstrates a spherical equivalent of -12.00 in both eyes. She and her mother both had cleft palates at birth, and her mother reports a history of retinal detachments in both eyes. What underlying genetic condition is most likely?
explanation: The abnormalities described are suggestive of Stickler syndrome. Ophthalmic ﬁndings of Stickler syndrome include high myopia, optically empty vitreous, congenital glaucoma, cataracts, and retinal detachment. Associated systemic ﬁndings include ﬂat midface, progressive hearing loss, Pierre Robin sequence (a series of anomalies caused by abnormal descent of the tongue, including cleft palate, glossoptosis, micrognathia, and respiratory problems), mitral valve prolapse, and progressive arthropathy. The most common type of Stickler syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a mutation in COL2A1, the gene that encodes for type II procollagen. A mutation in OPA1 is the most common cause of dominant optic atrophy, which is characterized clinically by a gradually progressive loss of visual acuity. question: What is the inheritance pattern of juvenile open-angle glaucoma (JOAG)?
explanation: Juvenile open-angle glaucoma (JOAG) is associated with the GLC1A myocilin gene (MYOC). It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is usually inherited as an autosomal recessive trait and associated with numerous genes, including GLC3A, GLC3B, GLC3D, LTBP2, and CYP1B1. Childhood glaucoma is not typically inherited as an X-linked recessive disease or as a mitochondrial disease. 9 50 per pa.

question: An infant is noted to have leukocoria, microphthalmos, and elongated ciliary processes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: All of the listed conditions (ROP, Coats disease, retinoblastoma) can present with leukocoria, but only persistent fetal vasculature is associated with microphthalmia. PFV results from failed regression of the fetal hyaloid vasculature. Findings can vary from a retrolental membrane to a stalk connecting the lens and optic nerve. It is also associated with elongated ciliary processes, cataract and retinal detachment, and angle closure glaucoma.

question: What initial therapy is used to treat the condition shown in this 7-day- old infant with Giemsa stain showing intracytoplasmic inclusions?
explanation: The photograph demonstrates a hyperacute conjunctivitis with purulent discharge in a newborn infant. This is neonatal conjunctivitis due to chlamydia, as evidenced by a Giemsa stain showing intracytoplasmic inclusions from a conjunctival scraping. The recommended treatment of chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum is systemic erythromycin (oral or intravenous), even though inclusion BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 35-year-old patient with cognitive impairment, adenoma sebaceum, and sharply delineated hypopigmented lesions on the skin, has the retinal lesion depicted in the image. On optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging, in what layer is the lesion present?
explanation: This is a retinal astrocytic hamartoma that is conﬁned to the nerve ﬁber layer. A retinal astrocytic hamartoma is a benign retinal tumor composed of glial cells, predominantly astrocytes. It is believed to be congenital in most cases, but it can become clinically apparent sometime after birth. Retinal astrocytoma may present as 1 or multiple lesions occurring unilaterally or bilaterally. In children, phakomas are relatively ﬂat, with a smooth surface, indistinct margins, and a gray- white color that makes them diﬃcult to detect. A second type of phakoma, more often found in adults, occurs adjacent to or on the optic nerve, with calciﬁed surface yielding a “mulberry” appearance. Retinal astrocytic hamartomas are frequently associated with tuberous sclerosis complex, a syndrome that includes various combinations of low-grade intracranial astrocytoma, cutaneous angioﬁbromas, cutaneous depigmented macules, cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma, and other hamartomas. The exact prevalence of retinal astrocytic hamartoma in tuberous sclerosis is not known. Approximately one-third to one-half of patients with tuberous sclerosis have retinal or optic nerve hamartoma, and in half of these, the hamartomas occur bilaterally. The tumor can be seen in patients with neuroﬁbromatosis as well. Clinically, the lesion can masquerade as a small retinoblastoma, but handheld OCT imaging can be used to demonstrate that the tumor is conﬁned to the nerve ﬁber layer.

question: Teller Acuity Cards II are likely to overestimate the vision in what eye condition?
explanation: Strabismic amblyopia has features that diﬀer from other types of amblyopia. Grating acuity, such as is tested with Teller Acuity Cards II and the LEA Grating Acuity Test, is reduced less than acuity measured with optotypes. Therefore, grating acuity can overestimate the vision. Linear LEA symbols, ETDRS (Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study) charts, and crowded HOTV charts accurately measure visual acuity in strabismic amblyopia. In refractive and deprivational amblyopia, this eﬀect is not seen. The presence of astigmatism does not aﬀect the accuracy of grating acuity measurements.

question: Following surgery for congenital cataract, what ﬁnding predisposes a child to glaucoma?
explanation: Aphakic glaucoma is a common form of secondary glaucoma in childhood. It often develops years after cataract surgery, but it can occur within weeks to months of surgery and is a lifelong risk. Those who have cataract surgery during infancy are at highest risk for glaucoma development, and the risk appears to be even higher in patients with microcornea or persistent fetal vasculature.

question: When operating on the inferior oblique muscle, damage to the associated nerve can cause what unwanted side eﬀect?
explanation: The nerve to the inferior oblique carries the pupillary parasympathetic ﬁbers; damage to this structure can cause an enlarged pupil. Anterior segment ischemia occurs when more than 2 rectus muscles are operated on at once, as they carry much of the blood supply to the anterior segment; the oblique muscles do not carry any blood to the anterior segment. Strabismus surgery on the inferior rectus muscle frequently causes widening or narrowing of the palpebral ﬁssure because of that muscle's fascial attachments to the lower lid; the inferior oblique does not have similar attachments. The nerves to the lacrimal gland are not typically encountered during strabismus surgery.

question: What is the most common genetic mutation associated with primary optic pathway gliomas in children?
explanation: Primary optic pathway gliomas in children are often associated with neuroﬁbromatosis type 1 (NF1) and therefore have a mutation on chromosome 17 (17q11.2). NF1 has an autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity. The associated glioma is a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma involving the optic nerve, chiasm, or both. Chiasmal glioma in patients with NF1 carries a better prognosis than in those without NF1. Primary optic nerve gliomas in children are not associated with 13q6.4 mutations, trisomy 13, or triploidy.

question: What additional eye motility abnormality do patients with infantile esotropia commonly have?

options.C: symmetric smooth pursuit in horizontal gaze

explanation: DVD is associated with infantile esotropia. Vertical nystagmus and ocular ﬂutter are not. Patients with infantile esotropia have asymmetric smooth pursuit, which is better in the temporal-to-nasal direction.

question: A previously healthy 6-year-old boy presents with rapid onset of unilateral painless proptosis. What is the most likely ﬁnding on microscopic examination of the orbital biopsy?

options.B: tissue derived from all 3 germinal layers

explanation: The most likely diagnosis for a 6-year-old child with unilateral, sudden- onset painless proptosis is rhabdomyosarcoma. The embryonal subtype shows a few cells with cross-striations on pathologic examination. Small, round blue cells are typical of neuroblastoma, which presents at a younger age; the average age of onset is 5-7 years. Dermoids have tissue from all 3 germ layers, but they are congenital and rarely present as sudden painless proptosis. options.A: superior rectus, medial rectus, inferior rectus, lateral rectus

question: An infant recently diagnosed with juvenile xanthogranuloma based on skin biopsy and presence of iris nodules is found not to have neuroﬁbromatosis. What can you tell the parents about the progression and prognosis of this condition?

options.A: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a progressive condition that will require ongoing treatment until early adulthood.
options.B: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a stable condition that can ﬂare up in adulthood.
options.C: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a self- limited condition that usually resolves spontaneously by the age of 5 years.
options.D: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a self- limited condition that begins to resolve in early adulthood.

explanation: Juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG) is a nonneoplastic histiocytic proliferation. It develops in children younger than 2 years and is characterized by Touton giant cells. Skin involvement is usually present and consists of small, round orange-tan papules. Iris lesions are relatively rare and almost always unilateral. question: What optic nerve ﬁnding may be seen in periventricular leukomalacia?
explanation: Periventricular leukomalacia is a prominent cause of cerebral (retrogeniculate) visual impairment (CVI), which is the most common cause of childhood visual impairment in developed countries.

question: The lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) can cause severe congenital infections. By what route or vector is the virus transmitted to the pregnant woman?
explanation: Rodents are the natural host and reservoir for LCMV. It is a single- stranded RNA virus of the Arenaviridae family; transmission to humans is often through exposure to rodents and thought to be airborne, possibly through food contamination or the rodent's bite. Ocular ﬁndings include macular and chorioretinal peripheral scarring, similar in morphology and distribution to that of congenital toxoplasmosis. Vertical transmission to a fetus occurs during episodes of maternal viremia. The earlier in gestation the transmission occurs, the more serious the sequelae. cycloplegics.

question: Intoxication with what class of eye drop would cause fever, ﬂushing, dry mouth, and delirium?
explanation: Cycloplegic agents are competitive antagonists of the muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Systemic intoxication includes fever, dry mouth, ﬂushing, rapid pulse, nausea, dizziness, delirium, and erythema. A common mnemonic used to describe the physiologic manifestations of atropine overdose is "hot as a pistol, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, and mad as a hatter." Adverse eﬀects of pilocarpine (a cholinergic) administration include miosis, retinal detachment, headache, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Beta blockers can cause bradycardia and bronchospasm. question: What is the eﬀect of a posterior ﬁxation suture in strabismus surgery?

options.A: redirecting the path of the muscle
options.B: strengthening of the muscle in its ﬁeld of action
options.C: weakening of the muscle in its ﬁeld of action

explanation: A posterior ﬁxation suture involves the attachment of a rectus muscle with a nonabsorbable suture 11-18 mm posterior to the insertion site and is used to weaken the muscle in its ﬁeld of action without signiﬁcantly aﬀecting alignment in primary position. This procedure is particularly useful for treatment of incomitant strabismus. Transposition procedures involve redirection of the paths of the extraocular muscles. Advancement of the anterior half of the superior oblique tendon reduces excyclotorsion in patients with superior oblique palsy.

question: A 9-year-old child with a history of recurrent bacterial infections develops an intractable respiratory infection that proves fatal. The ocular and histopathologic ﬁndings of the patient are shown in the ﬁgure below. What is the most likely underlying disease in this patient?
explanation: The ocular ﬁndings as shown in the above ﬁgure, iris transillumination defects, fundus hypopigmentation, and decreased melanin distribution in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choroidal tissue are consistent with ocular albinism. Two notable syndromes associated with ocular-cutaneous albinism are Chédiak-Higashi syndrome and Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome. Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder with a mutation in a lysosomal traﬃcking regulator protein that renders inadequate phagocytosis. This results in recurrent pyogenic infections, often involving the respiratory and cutaneous systems. Patients with Chédiak-Higashi syndrome rarely survive past 10 years of age and often succumb to infection. Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by ocular-cutaneous albinism and bleeding problems from a platelet abnormality. Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder of metabolism involving glucocerebroside. Gaucher disease is not associated with albinism. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) is a rare progressive genetic disorder characterized by an inability of the body to transport cholesterol and other fatty substances (lipids) inside of cells.

question: A physician has examined a child and decided to perform a primary enucleation for the treatment of retinoblastoma. What clinical ﬁnding may have led to this decision?

options.B: single small tumor behind the equator
options.D: single small tumor anterior to the equator

explanation: In advanced unilateral retinoblastoma, when the likelihood of saving any vision is low, primary enucleation is recommended. question: A 1-year-old child presents for evaluation of constant, large-angle exotropia that has been present since birth. Aside from a complete ophthalmic examination, what additional piece of information is crucial to obtain?
explanation: Infantile exotropia (XT) presents before age 6 months with a large- angle, constant exodeviation. Patients who are otherwise healthy (no ocular or systemic disease) are classiﬁed as having primary infantile XT. However, one must consider secondary causes, as patients with infantile XT are at increased risk of associated neurologic impairment or developmental delay. Referral for neurologic assessment may be necessary if there are concerns about neurologic or developmental delay. As mentioned in the question stem, a complete ophthalmic examination, including a dilated fundus examination, is required in new patients with strabismus, as XT may also result from retinal or optic nerve abnormalities. Patients with eso or exo deviations often have a family history of strabismus, however, this knowledge is not necessary or crucial to further care. Monocular occlusion testing is helpful when evaluating BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 4-year-old boy presents with an orbital mass. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan is performed, and orbital lymphatic malformation (previously known as lymphangioma) is diagnosed. What other information may be obtained to support the diagnosis?

options.B: reddish color of the orbital lesion
options.D: exacerbation of symptoms with upper respiratory infection

explanation: Orbital lymphatic malformations (previously known as lymphangiomas) often contain venous and lymphatic components, and it may enlarge during upper respiratory tract infections because of the response of the lymphoid tissues within the lesion. Sudden hemorrhage from interstitial capillaries may present with abrupt proptosis; thus, normal exophthalmometer measurement does not conﬁrm or negate the diagnosis. These malformations are best managed conservatively, but partial resection and drainage may be necessary if vision is threatened. Complete removal is usually impossible due to the inﬁltrative nature of the lesion.

question: A 2-year-old child presents with a 30° right head turn. The patient cannot abduct the right eye, and there is narrowing of the palpebral ﬁssure on adduction. Dilated funduscopic examination is normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and brainstem

explanation: The patient described has type 1 Duane retraction syndrome. A medial rectus recession on the aﬀected side would correct the head turn and centralize the ﬁeld of binocular vision. While limited abduction may be a result of a sixth nerve palsy, globe retraction causing narrowing of the palpebral ﬁssures is diagnostic of Duane retraction syndrome. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is thus not necessary for further evaluation of a sixth nerve palsy; aberrant regeneration from a compressive lesion is unlikely in a 2-year-old, and if associated with the third nerve would result in widening of the palpebral ﬁssure with or without miosis rather than narrowing of the palpebral ﬁssure. A lumbar puncture to check for elevated intracranial pressure, which may be indicated in the presence of a sixth nerve palsy, is also not indicated, especially with a normal dilated fundus examination. A muscle biopsy for strabismus is used in cases of suspected chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) to evaluate for ragged red ﬁbers or mitochondrial DNA changes. A child with CPEO would be expected to present with ptosis and limitation of eye movements but not globe retraction.

question: What method is recommended for assessing the refractive state in children with amblyopia?
explanation: Cycloplegic retinoscopy is the most objective and accurate method to determine the ocular refractive state in amblyopia. Due to the large accommodative capacity and tone in children, cycloplegia is necessary to accurately determine the full refractive error, especially in patients with hyperopia. Therapy for refractive amblyopia is predicated upon correcting the full refractive error of the amblyopic eye(s) and penalizing the least amblyopic or non-amblyopic eye. Because an amblyopic eye’s ability to control accommodation tends to be impaired, this eye cannot be relied on to compensate for uncorrected hyperopia as would a normal child’s eye. Retinoscopy under anesthesia (but without complete cycloplegia), manifest refraction, and autorefraction are not satisfactory, because they may not determine the full optical refractive state in the highly accommodative pediatric eye. optic nerve glioma.

question: Persistent fetal vasculature is associated with what extraocular abnormality?
explanation: The reduced visual acuity that may be associated with persistent fetal vasculature may in turn lead to the development of sensory strabismus. Patients whose vision is lost or impaired at birth are more likely to develop esotropia, whereas patients with acquired vision loss or impairment later in life mostly develop exotropia. question: What would be the most likely ﬁndings in a 15-month-old patient diagnosed with congenital ﬁbrosis syndrome?

options.A: bilateral proptosis and limitations of abduction
options.B: ptosis and decreased extraocular movements that vary day to day
options.C: unilateral ptosis with limitation of adduction
options.D: bilateral ptosis and limitations of vertical eye movements

explanation: Congenital ﬁbrosis syndrome or congenital ﬁbrosis of the extraocular muscles (CFEOM) is a group of conditions within the general category of congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders caused by primary dysinnervation of the extraocular muscles. Congenital ﬁbrosis syndrome leads to replacement of sparsely innervated muscle by ﬁbrous tissue. Congenital ﬁbrosis syndrome must be diﬀerentiated from thyroid eye disease, myasthenia gravis, 3rd nerve palsy, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO). Thyroid eye disease would more likely present with proptosis and lid retraction with limitations of extraocular eye movements. Myasthenia gravis may present with ptosis and progressive decrease in extraocular movements, and this would be variable from day to day. Superior rectus weakness or overaction are recognized associations and contribute to causing vertical deviations. Progressive loss of extraocular movements over years would be consistent with CPEO. A third nerve palsy may present with unilateral or bilateral ptosis and limitation of adduction, along with limitation of supra- and infraduction while abduction is intact. Möbius syndrome will have facial nerve weakness, and vertical motility will be intact.

question: A 1-year-old child presents with a bright red lesion of the upper eyelid that has existed since birth but has recently been enlarging in size. There is mild, symmetric astigmatism in both eyes. The mother insists on treatment to remove the entire lesion. What is the best treatment option?
explanation: Capillary hemangiomas are common eyelid lesions in children. These may appear at or shortly after birth and clinically appear as bright red lesions that grow rapidly over weeks to months. These lesions are nonencapsulated and usually involute spontaneously. Histologic appearance depends on the stage. Early lesions show sheets of benign endothelial cells surrounding capillary channels. Involuting lesions display increased ﬁbrosis and hyalinization of capillary walls. Although lesions eventually involute and regress, they can pose a risk for amblyopia. β-blockers are often used as ﬁrst-line treatment of capillary hemangiomas, usually with signiﬁcant reduction in size. Excision of these lesions should be performed with care because it can lead to signiﬁcant blood loss from the large feeder vessels that are present BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What congenital iris abnormality represents a sequestration of epithelium during embryologic development?

options.B: cyst of the iris pigment epithelium

explanation: Iris stromal cysts are enlarging congenital lesions that are caused by sequestration of epithelial tissues during embryogenesis. Due to enlargement, they may cause visual obstruction, glaucoma, and corneal decompensation. Cysts of the iris pigment epithelium are caused by separation of the 2 layers of the iris pigment epithelium, not by sequestration of tissue. They typically are stable and do not usually cause clinical complications. Pigment epithelial cysts at the pupil border, also referred to as central cysts, can be hereditary. Although they sometimes enlarge slowly, they rarely cause complications. Lisch nodules are hamartomas of the iris that are present in patients with neuroﬁbromatosis type 1.

question: What is the most appropriate approach to a left hypertropia occurring after a left orbital ﬂoor fracture without entrapment?

options.C: right inferior rectus posterior ﬁxation suture

explanation: A patient with a left hypertropia after a left orbital ﬂoor fracture without entrapment most likely has weakness or palsy of the left inferior rectus. Initial management should be observation, as the weakness may improve with time. If recovery is not complete within 6–12 months of the injury and there is at least a moderate degree of active force, resection of the aﬀected muscle can be performed. If the hypertropia is large, the procedure can be combined with recession of the ipsilateral superior rectus muscle or recession of the contralateral inferior rectus muscle, with or without the addition of a posterior ﬁxation suture (fadenoperation). Transposition of the ipsilateral medial and lateral rectus muscles to the inferior rectus muscle (inverse Knapp procedure) may be necessary for treatment of complete, chronic inferior rectus muscle palsy or when a crippling amount of recession has been necessary to relieve restriction.
